full_name: ISO/IEC 19566-5:2023. Information technologies - JPEG systems - Part 5: JPEG universal metadata box format (JUMBF)
short_description: JPEG Universal Metadata Box Format (JUMBF) is a standardized format to embed metadata and auxiliary data within or outside of JPEG image files and other box-based formats.
description: JPEG universal metadata box format (JUMBF) is an ISO/IEC standardized format designed for embedding and referencing arbitrary metadata and auxiliary data in JPEG image files. It uses a box-based hierarchical structure to store metadata, binary data, JSON, XML, UUIDs, embedded files, or other data, and supports both embedding metadata directly inside the JPEG (via JPEG XT's APP11 mechanism for JPEG-1) and referencing or requesting metadata internally or externally. This structure mirrors the box-based model defined by 14496-12 ISO base media format (ISOBMFF), enabling compatibility with the JPEG family and other box-based formats. As stated in ISO/ICE 19566-5:2023, "The annexes of this document focus on the definition of boxes. The details for embedding boxes in specific file formats are defined in the particular documents, for example ISO/IEC 15444-1 for JPEG 2000, ISO/IEC 18477-3 for JPEG-1 / JPEG XT or the more generic ISO/IEC 14496-12 ISO base media format (ISO_BMFF)" (ISO/ICE 19566-5:2023, page 3. Section 4.3 Boxes and superboxes). Paraphrasing the standard document, Annex A of the 2nd edition of the standard, provides an informative overview of the JUMBF box file format and technical structure. Annex B describes JUMBF Content Types; Annex C describes the mechanism for referencing and requesting the embedded data, internally or externally to the image; and Annex D describes backwards compatibility and methods for embedding JUMBF Boxes using the JPEG XT Box Format (ISO/ICE 19566-5:2023, page 4). The following is a summary of the structural information defined in Annex A, as presented in the openly available sample of ISO/ICE 19566-5:2023 as of June 22, 2026: A JUMBF file is organized as a hierarchy of boxes in a binary format where each box encapsulates metadata objects; JUMBF defines a specific superbox type (jumb) that contains other boxes according to the standard. See Figure A1 in the specification for a structure diagram (publicly visible in the 2019 edition sample of the standard). Inside a jumb superbox, there is exactly one JUMBF Description Box, followed by one or more JUMBF Content Boxes that carry the metadata payload, plus an optional padding box. This nested structure is self-describing and extensible. When embedded inside a JPEG-1 file, a JUMBF Super Box utilizes the JPEG XT Box File Format, which is identified by marker segment APP11, and is self-describing via the structural elements Description Box, content type UUID, labels, IDs etc. (See Diaz, Carlos Valverde. "JPEG Universal Metadata Box Format and JPEG Linked Media Format: a Reference Software Implementation", 2022, p. 20).

sustainability.disclosure: International standard, fully disclosed.
sustainability.documentation: Published as ISO/IEC 19566-5:2023 - Information technologies — JPEG systems Part 5: JPEG universal metadata box format (JUMBF), with an amendment published as of March 2025, and a further draft under development as of June 2026: ISO/IEC 19566-5:2023 - Information technologies — JPEG systems Part 5: JPEG universal metadata box format (JUMBF). ISO/IEC 19566-5:2023/Amd 1:2025 - JUMBF box compression and standalone JUMBF files ISO/IEC CD 19566-5 - Information technology — JPEG Systems Part 5: JPEG universal metadata box format (JUMBF)
sustainability.adoption: As of 2026, notable implementations of JUMBF include its adoption as a primary container format for implementation of the Content Authenticity and Provenance (C2PA) Content Credentials specification for embedding provenance information, and within the JPEG 360 standard for omni-directional images (see ISO/IEC 19566-6:2026 - JPEG systems - Part 6: JPEG 360). In the context of C2PA, JUMBF is leveraged to store manifests or other sidecar data specific to various content types which detail creation, modification, and other authenticity information (see C2PA Technical Specification, 10.1 - Use of JUMBF for a general overview on the C2PA Manifest Store structure as it pertains to JUMBF). Within JPEG 360, JUMBF is similarly used as a mechanism for storing manifests, in this case 360-degree image metadata (see Kim, Yoonjoung; Choi, Yongjun; Nam, Younga; Kim, Sanghoon; Generation of a Panorama Compatible with the JPEG 360 International Standard Using a Single PTZ Camera, Section 3.3). Some academic and software implementation projects have also explored or begun implementing JUMBF, such as integration of JUMBF with JLINK (see Valverde Diaz, 2022). Some reference software and libraries also exist. Comments welcome
sustainability.transparency: Depends upon usage. Renderability of embedded or sidecar data depends on tool support; data contained within a JUMBF metadata box will be ignored if the rendering tool cannot recognize the data.
sustainability.selfDocumentation: When embedded inside a JPEG file, a JUMBF Super Box utilizes the JPEG XT Box File Format, which is identified by marker segment APP11, and is self-describing via the structural elements Description Box, content type UUID, labels, IDs etc. (See Diaz, Carlos Valverde. "JPEG Universal Metadata Box Format and JPEG Linked Media Format: a Reference Software Implementation", 2022, p. 20). Accessibility Features JUMBF has no specific attributes to support accessibility at this time. There may be applications for enhancing accessibility through the use of JUMBF to store data that supports use of accessibility tools, but documentation is limited at this time. Features to support accessibility would be found in associated files (such as embedded captions and subtitles in audiovisual content, tagged and structured text in textual documents, and alt text for images). Aggregate files can also contain separate files for transcripts, timed text or captions as part of the bundled package. See Relationships to other formats for details. Comments welcome.
sustainability.externalDependencies: There are no proprietary dependencies for implementation, but renderability of any stored data is dependent on the capability of applicable rendering or reporting software.

relationships.comment: JPEG 360, not described separately at this time.

short_description: TOML (Tom's Obvious, Minimal Language) is a purposefully minimal open source configuration file format with obvious semantics designed for unambiguous human understanding.
description: TOML (Tom's Obvious, Minimal Language) is a purposefully minimal configuration file format with obvious semantics designed for unambiguous human understanding. It's an open source format and originally created by Tom Preston-Werner, co-founder of GitHub. The TOML specification is hosted at https://toml.io/en/. See Documentation and History for more details about versions. As described on the TOML Project homepage, TOML's specific features to support human interaction include a collection of useful native types (Key/Value Pairs, Arrays, Inline tables, Arrays of tables, Integers and Floats, Booleans, Dates and Times, with optional offsets) and the fact that TOML is designed to map unambiguously to a hash table. TOML files are case sensitive and have the option to make generous use of comments, identified with a hash symbol, to communicate between the human readers of a file. Key Value pairs are the building block of TOML structured with keys are on the left of the equals sign and values are on the right, i.e. key = "value". Values must be from a controlled vocabulary list of options and non-recognized values are ignored. Each value option (String; Integer; Float; Boolean; Offset Date-Time; Local Date-Time; Local Date; Local Time; Array; Inline Table) has additional specific parameters. A few highlights include that String must be UNICODE, Date options must comply with RFC 3339: Date and Time on the Internet: Timestamps and Tables are defined by headers which, in addition to other goals, assist with accessibility support. In general, TOML files must be UTF-8 encoded Unicode, whitespace is ignored and TOML is case-sensitive. Also TOML files can make liberal use of comments to explain specific parts of the context to other human readers. Structurally, "a hash symbol marks the rest of the line as a comment, except when inside a string."

sustainability.disclosure: Fully documented and open. Current version in 2026 is v.1.1.0 and documentation for all versions is available. There's also an active open Wiki for the community to catalog various TOML-related projects.
sustainability.documentation: TOML, version 1.1.0, Dec 18, 2025. All previous specification versions fully available via toml.io as HTML and TEXT and the https://github.com/toml-lang/toml GitHub repository includes information on TOML's syntax using the Augmented Backus–Naur Form (ABNF) format.
sustainability.adoption: Widely adopted. Implementations by supported version are listed in GitHub and include most of the most popular programming languages such as C, C#, C++, Clojure, Dart, Elixir, Erlang, Go, Haskell, Java, JavaScript, Lua, Objective-C, Perl, PHP, Python, Ruby, Rust, Scala, SML, Swift, V and Zig among others. One application is in the RUST Library, part of the Content Authenticity Initiative (CAI) open-source SDK to implement Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity or C2PA Content Credentials (v2.3 as of this writing in March 2026).
sustainability.licensingAndPatents: TOML is released under an MIT License: a permissive license with conditions only requiring preservation of copyright and license notices. Licensed works, modifications, and larger works may be distributed under different terms and without source code. Copyright is held by Tom Preston-Werner.
sustainability.transparency: TOML must be a valid UTF-8 encoded Unicode document. Specifically this means that a file as a whole must form a well-formed code-unit sequence. Otherwise, it must be rejected (preferably) or have ill-formed byte sequences replaced with U+FFFD, as per the Unicode specification.
sustainability.selfDocumentation: The TOML format prioritizes human readability, simple syntax, and easy editing through clear key/value pairs. As plain text files, they work in any editor, avoid complex indentation issues, and map directly to dictionaries. Accessibility Features TOML does support accessibility because, being text-based, files can be read by screen readers and complex structures can be explained with labeled comments. Also the unambiguous structure of the key-value pairs (key = value) and tables ([table]) can be easy to parse and interpret. Tables include headers which help organize information for adaptive technologies.

full_name: JPEG XT - ISO/IEC 18477 Information technology — Scalable compression and coding of continuous-tone still images
short_description: JPEG XT (a contraction of JPEG eXTension) is a backwards compatible extension of JPEG with support for higher bit depths (9 to 16 bits), high-dynamic-range imaging, lossless compression, and representation of alpha channels.
description: JPEG XT (a contraction of 'JPEG eXTension') is a series of backward compatible extensions to the legacy JPEG (ISO 10918) format and offers the ability to encode images of higher precision and higher dynamic range, and in lossy or lossless modes. JPEG XT is defined in nine parts of ISO/IEC 18477 through the ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 29 working group in collaboration with Joint Photographic Experts Group (JPEG) (jpeg.org). See Documentation for details on the various parts that define the standard. The unique features of JPEG XT, in addition to backwards compatibility with earlier forms of JPEG, are support for higher bit depths (9 to 16 bits), high-dynamic-range imaging, lossless compression, and representation of alpha channels. Structurally, and in line with other forms of JPEG, JPEG XT is a subtype of the ISO Base Media File Format or ISO BMFF (ISO/IEC 14496-12. Information technology -- Coding of audio-visual objects -- Part 12: ISO Base Media File Format. Part of MPEG-4) in which all data is encapsulated in boxes and the specifics for JPEG XT are defined in SO/IEC 18477I-3. The ISO_BMFF mechanism for distinguishing among file types is based on 4-character codes known as 'brands', either major or minor brands; brands are registered with the MP4 Registration Authority. At or near the beginning of a file will be the mandatory file-type box, with type ftyp. This box can specify values for major-brand, minor-brand, and compatible-brands. The major brand usually implies the file extension, which in turn implies the MIME type for the file. However, as of May 2026, 'JPXT' or JPEG XT is not registered as a brand. Comments welcome. There are three algorithms for reconstructing the HDR image (defined in ISO/IEC 18477-7) and further described in JPEG XT: A New Family of JPEG Backward-Compatible Standards: Profile A: Uses a simple, common logarithmic scale factor to reconstruct the HDR image from the base layer. The HDR image is described as the pixel-wise product of an inversely gammacorrected 8-bit tone-mapped image multiplied by a common scale factor, not quite unlike the RGBE format. The scale factor is encoded in logarithmic space—that is, it’s also an exponent as in the RGBE representation. In addition to the RGBE format, Profile A also includes an additive chroma residual that allows correction of color defects that might arise due to simple scaling. Profile B: Uses a divisor image (an extension layer) scaled by a common exposure value for reconstruction. In this profile, the HDR image is described as the pixel-wise quotient of the inversely gamma-corrected tone-mapped image and a divisor image delivered by the extension layer. The output is additionally scaled by one common factor, the “exposure value.” Profile C: Similar to Profile A, but employs per-component scaling factors, allowing for higher precision, often used for 12-bit extensions (8-bit legacy + 4-bit refinement). Profile C works almost like Profile A—that is, it decomposes the image into an 8-bit image and scale factors, except that here each component has its individual scale factor, whereas in Profile A, there’s only a single common scale factor. Profile C also performs the multiplication as an addition in logarithmic space. Profile D: This profile is not for coding HDR images and does not assume the residual layer. The profile is provided only to simply extend the dynamic range of the traditional LDR image encoded by the L-JPEG. The choice of the profile is open to users. Each profile is differentiated by how it specifies a subset of the functional blocks for reconstructing the output HDR image. A fourth, Profile D, is not for coding HDR images. As Wikipedia JPEG XT entry explains, "the enhancement layer is used to store extended precision of discrete cosine transform (DCT) transfer coefficients, and non-gamma transfer function is applied to increase dynamic range to 12 bits. Backward compatibility is limited because legacy decoders do not understand new EOTF curves and produce undersaturated colors. Profile D is not implemented in reference software." As noted in JPEG XT: A New Family of JPEG Backward-Compatible Standards, "JPEG XT also allows mixing of profiles, so some elements from Profile C can be mixed into a Profile B configuration, or the Profile D extension of the precision of the DCT samples can improve the extension layer in Profile C. The resulting codestreams are then called "full profile" codestreams because their configuration exceed the constraints implied by a single profile, though such streams are fully covered by the JPEG XT standard."

sustainability.disclosure: Fully disclosed. Developed by the Joint Photographic Experts Group (JPEG) committee (ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 29/WG 1). See About JPEG.
sustainability.documentation: JPEG XT is defined in nine parts through ISO/IEC 18477 Information technology — Scalable compression and coding of continuous-tone still images. These are updated regularly so a good place to track the most current versions is Workplan & Specs of JPEG XT from jpeg.org. Links to the current ISO versions as of April 2026 are listed in Format specifications. ISO/IEC 18477-1:2024: Core coding system specification ISO/IEC 18477-2:2016: Coding of high dynamic range images ISO/IEC 18477-3:2023: Box file format ISO/IEC 18477-4:2017: Conformance testing ISO/IEC 18477-4:2017/Cor 1:2023: Conformance testing — Technical Corrigendum 1 ISO/IEC 18477-5:2018: Reference software ISO/IEC 18477-6:2016: IDR Integer Coding ISO/IEC 18477-7:2017: HDR Floating-Point Coding ISO/IEC 18477-8:2020: Lossless and near-lossless coding ISO/IEC 18477-9:2016: Alpha channel coding
sustainability.adoption: Reference software is available from both the ISO reference implementation and third party contributors on jpeg.org's Software for JPEG XT page.
sustainability.licensingAndPatents: Starting in April 2019, Sisvel had licensed the JPEG-XT patents that were owned by Dolby International AB (affiliate of Dolby Laboratories, Inc.) and Trellis Europe S.r.l. but, as of 2026, this is no longer active.
sustainability.transparency: Depends upon algorithms and tools to read; will require sophistication to build tools. JPEG XT supports encryption which is incompatible with transparency. As stated in JPEG Privacy and Security Abstract and Executive Summary, "in a simple extension of JPEG XT, it would be only necessary to encrypt the extension layer. In the simplest possible realization, both base and extension layer would be 8 bits per component images, both encoded in JPEG — such an arrangement is already covered by JPEG XT part 6. Image regions could be pixelated or of lower quality in the base layer, while the (encrypted) extension layer would carry the differential signal between intended full-quality image and the degraded base image."
sustainability.selfDocumentation: See JPEG (ISO 10918) and JFIF_Family Accessibility Features JPEG XT has no specific attributes to support accessibility. JPEG XT allows for lossy and lossless alpha channels (transparency) in Part 9. While this is excellent for design elements like non-rectangular logos or overlapping visual elements, it does not provide semantic information for assistive technologies. Comments welcome. Accessibility for still image content is often supported by the use of alt text when displayed on the web. The carriage of this data is typically not embedded in the file itself but rather in the HTML code. See W3C's Text alternatives for non-text content for more information.

relationships.related_title: ISO/IEC 14496-12. Information technology -- Coding of audio-visual objects -- Part 12: ISO Base Media File Format (formal name). ISO base media file format (common name)

relationships.comment: Not separately described at this time. The JPEG XT file format can be used to embed JUMBF boxes in JPEG-1 images (ITU-T.81|ISO/IEC 10918-1)

JPEG XT Part 3 specifies an extensible boxed-based file format all following and future extensions of JPEG will be based on. The format specified in Part 3 is itself compatible to JFIF, ISO/IEC 10918-5, and thus can be read by all existing implementations.

short_description: Inside-Outside-Beginning (IOB, or BIO) is the standard tagging format used to represent chunk structures from a corpus for natural language processing tasks.
description: Inside-Outside-Beginning (IOB, or sometimes BIO) is a tagging format used to represent the structure of non-overlapping phrases, also called chunks or spans, in a large body of text, or corpus. It is commonly used in natural language processing tasks, such as named entity recognition (NER), to structure data for further analysis. According to the 2019 book Natural Language Processing with Python, "IOB tags have become the standard way to represent chunk structures in files." IOB tags are applied to each word in a corpus: B if the word is the beginning of a phrase, I if inside a phrase, or O if outside a phrase. IOB tags can be used on their own or together with other tags, such as part-of-speech tags or named entity types (e.g., person, organization, location, date, etc.). Variations of IOB There is no formal specification for IOB tags. They were proposed by Lance A. Ramshaw and Mitchell P. Marcus to encode base noun phrase (baseNP) chunks and documented in their 1995 paper Text Chunking using Transformation-Based Learning: "[W]e use the chunk tag set {I, O, B}, where words marked I are inside some baseNP, those marked O are outside, and the B tag is used to mark the left most item of a baseNP which immediately follows another baseNP." Ramshaw and Marcus’ method was dubbed "IOB1" by Erik Tjong Kim Sang and Jorn Veenstra in their 1999 paper Representing Text Chunks, wherein they also propose IOB2. In IOB2, the first word of all noun phrase chunks receives a B tag, not just those that immediately follow another noun phrase. IOB2 is the more common variant, and according to AI expert Michael Brenndoerfer, "All modern benchmarks use IOB2." See Notes below for discussion of additional IOB variants. IOB Representation IOB is typically represented in a text file, separate from the corpus, using a column-based format. According to Tjong Kim Sang, Ramshaw and Marcus formatted their IOB data with each line of the file containing a word from the corpus, its part-of-speech tag, its IOB tag, and three other undescribed fields. In the early 2000s, the Conference on Computational Natural Language Learning (CoNLL) had a series of shared tasks that used IOB tagging (proceedings available in the ACL Anthology), which necessitated having a common representation for IOB that would "allow for multiple annotations over the same data" and "be easily machine-processable by diverse teams and software," per the Handbook of Linguistic Annotation. According to Brenndoerfer, "The CoNLL-2003 dataset... set the template that most NER datasets have followed since." The CoNLL-2003 format, as described in Introduction to the CoNLL-2003 Shared Task: Language-Independent Named Entity Recognition, contains one line for each word in the corpus with four columns, each separated by a space: the word, its part-of-speech tag, its syntactic chunk tag, and its named entity tag. Chunk and named entity tags have the format I- or B-TYPE, or O. Empty lines represent sentence boundaries. Because of their column-based representation, IOB tags can only represent non-overlapping chunks; they cannot represent nested or discontiguous chunks. Per the Handbook of Linguistic Annotation, "[The column-based format] does not readily handle hierarchical annotations (e.g., syntax trees) or annotation of discontiguous tokens. As with inline XML, co-indexing is required to specify hierarchical relations or relate discontiguous items, and such co-indexing substantially complicates the processing of documents in this format."

sustainability.disclosure: Non-proprietary and not formally documented.
sustainability.documentation: See Ramshaw and Marcus' Text Chunking using Transformation-Based Learning and Tjong Kim Sang and Veenstra's Representing Text Chunks papers for descriptions of IOB1 and IOB2. For documentation on CoNLL-2003 representation of IOB, consult Introduction to the CoNLL-2003 Shared Task: Language-Independent Named Entity Recognition.
sustainability.adoption: According to the book Natural Language Processing with Python, "The most widespread file representation [of chunk structures] uses IOB tags." The authors of this book also developed the Natural Language Toolkit (NLTK), a free open-source platform for using Python to perform natural language processing tasks on corpora. The toolkit includes some existing IOB-tagged corpora, like CoNLL 2000 and 2002, and functions for working with the IOB format. According to the Handbook of Linguistic Annotation, "The [CoNLL IOB] format’s simplicity, ease of processing, and human readability have made CoNLL a popular format despite the awkwardness of representing certain types of information (e.g., syntactic hierarchies). At the same time, due to its popularity, transducers to and from CoNLL format for some general-purpose formats exist." In addition to the NLTK, some natural language processing tools that can work with IOB include spaCy, Nestor, INCEpTION, and iobes, among others.
sustainability.transparency: IOB tags are human readable in a text editor.
sustainability.selfDocumentation: Wikipedia's IOB article says, "IOB files have no place to put commonly-needed [metadata], such as the character encoding being used, the data source, internal location-markers, and so on." The Handbook of Linguistic Annotation also points out that one disadvantage of representing IOB in a column-based format is "that the columns need to be interpreted: their role is not made explicit in the representation as it is, for example, in the element names and attributes of an XML format, and users of the format need to agree on what information goes where." Supporting documentation for an annotated corpus may contain such information. Accessibility Features Other than being represented in a structured, column-based text file, IOB tags have no specific attributes to support accessibility. Comments welcome.

short_description: Open source bitstream encoding format designed for lossless compression of LPCM audio data, with many of its default parameters tuned to CD-quality music data.
description: FLAC (Free Lossless Audio Codec) is a bitstream encoding format designed for lossless compression of PCM audio data. The FLAC specification is open and fully documented specification published through IETF RFC 9639. According to xiph.org, FLAC lists a number of high level features including support for lossless compression and content authenticity: "The encoding of audio (PCM) data incurs no loss of information, and the decoded audio is bit-for-bit identical to what went into the encoder. Each frame contains a 16-bit CRC of the frame data for detecting transmission errors. The integrity of the audio data is further insured by storing an MD5 signature of the original unencoded audio data in the file header, which can be compared against later during decoding or testing." Other attributes include faster processing speed ("FLAC is asymmetric in favor of decode speed. Decoding requires only integer arithmetic, and is much less compute-intensive than for most perceptual codecs") and flexible metadata including support for cue sheets (see Self Documentation) with many of its default parameters tuned to CD-quality music data. The data structure is described in Notes, below. The format also includes "transport system" elements that provide a file format for the encoded data. The FLAC xiph.org indicates that in some applications there may be advantages to using Ogg (or Matroska) as a wrapper. Comments welcome.

sustainability.disclosure: Fully documented and open. See History, below.
sustainability.documentation: IETF Drafts, starting with 2017 as well as the final RFC 9639, are available on the IETF Data Tracker: Free Lossless Audio Codec (FLAC). Earlier documentation is available through xiph downloads and SourceForge. See Notes for full version history.
sustainability.adoption: xiph.org includes a list of diverse FLAC resources but this may not be current. On the commercial side, Amazon Music supports FLAC "to deliver HD and UHD audio." FLAC is widely supported across major web browsers. The IETF Cellar Working Group also provides a set of FLAC test files. The DPC Technology Watch Guidance Note Preserving Audio (July 2021) states that "FLAC is not as widely used as WAV due to the fact that it is a newer format, is less established in a preservation context, and has less explicit tool support. However, it is considered an acceptable preservation format." Overall, FLAC is gaining adoption in the audio digital preservation communities. For example, the US National Archives and Records Administration includes FLAC v.1.2.1 on its preferred formats for digital audio for Transfer Guidance (as of June 2026) and the Smithsonian Institution Archives includes it as an acceptable format on its list of Recommended Preservation Formats for Electronic Records. It's also mentioned in the ARSC Guide to Audio Preservation (2015). See also FLAC Family.
sustainability.licensingAndPatents: Documentation and tools are freely distributed under Xiph's variant of the BSD open-source license. No known patents.
sustainability.transparency: Depends upon algorithms and tools to read; requires sophistication to build tools.
sustainability.selfDocumentation: RFC 9639 states: "A FLAC bitstream consists of the fLaC (i.e., 0x664C6143) marker at the beginning of the stream, followed by a mandatory metadata block (called the streaminfo metadata block), any number of other metadata blocks, and then the audio frames. FLAC supports 127 kinds of metadata blocks; ... [The STREAMINFO block] The streaminfo metadata block has information about the whole stream, such as sample rate, number of channels, total number of samples, etc. It MUST be present as the first metadata block in the stream. Other metadata blocks MAY follow. There MUST be no more than one streaminfo metadata block per FLAC stream." Also included in the STREAMINFO block is the MD5 signature of the unencoded audio data. From https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9639.html#name-cuesheet: A cuesheet metadata block can be used either to store the track and index point structure of a Compact Disc Digital Audio (CD-DA) along with its audio or to provide a mechanism to store locations of interest within a FLAC file. Certain aspects of this metadata block come directly from the CD-DA specification (called Red Book), which is standardized as [IEC.60908.1999]. Accessibility Features FLAC's metadata support allows for comprehensive tagging of album info, lyrics, and track titles that may be accessible to screen readers. In common practice, typically audio content is supported by external caption and subtitle formats such as WebVTT. See W3C's Making Audio and Video Media Accessible for more general information about accessible sound and moving image media.

relationships.comment: FLAC is often used with the Matroska container.
Wikipedia states that FLAC is supported in CAF containers. Comments welcome.
FLAC files and streams can code for pulse-code modulated (PCM) audio.
